files.title: Context file
files.body:
# AGENTS.md — {{initiative}}

> Node SDLC · Act VII OPERATE · Scale: Solo / small. Read this first, every session.

## How we work
People own the work, agents help do it. In every unit the person in the role briefs the agent, gives it the right context, checks what it produces, and makes every decision. The agent drafts, researches, analyses, structures and checks — it never decides, approves or signs.
- **You:** Choose what to work on · give context · make decisions · review and correct · sign off · own the artifact
- **Your agent:** Draft · research · summarise · structure into templates · spot gaps and risks · check against criteria · prepare options

## Where this act sits
OPERATE is part of the **Run & learn** — Is it working, and what did we learn? The acts keep their order as a logical dependency — a problem is validated before it is planned, designed before it is built — but they are kinds of work that run continuously and in parallel, at different sizes, not phases on a calendar.

## OPERATE: Run the service reliably, securely and economically; respond to failure; and turn what running it teaches into signals the next cycle can act on.
- **7.1 Observability & Monitoring** — gate: SLO & Error Budget. Produces: SLO specification, Error-budget policy, Service dashboard, Alert rules, On-call rota, Error-budget report, Release freeze notice, Operations signal digest, Operations signal pack.
- **7.2 Incident Management** — gate: Service Restored. Produces: Incident record, Incident status update, Incident timeline, Hotfix request, Postmortem, Problem record.
- **7.3 Problem Management** — gate: Problem Review. Produces: Problem record, Problem investigation, Known-error record, Knowledge-base article, Product backlog entry, Fix verification.
- **7.4 Service Request & Support** — gate: Support Service Review. Produces: Service catalogue, Support model, Service request, Feedback record, Knowledge-base article, Support report.
- **7.5 Capacity & Cost** — gate: Capacity & Cost Review. Produces: Demand forecast, Capacity plan, Load-test results, Cost-to-serve report, Optimisation log.
- **7.6 Security Operations** — gate: Security Posture Review. Produces: Vulnerability register, Detection rule catalogue, Security event record, Breach notification, Access review, Security posture report, Hotfix request.
- Act gate: **SLO & Error Budget** — decided by: Service owner applies the error-budget policy and lifts freezes; incident commander directs incidents; product owner ranks problem fixes; DPO decides breach notification..

## Conventions
- Artifacts live in `docs/<artifact>.md`, written from `templates/<artifact>.md`.
- Every artifact carries its trace ID and links the IDs upstream of it; register new IDs in `TRACE.md`.
- Trace chain: SLO → ALR → INC → PM → PRB → KE → SR → CAP → VUL → EBR → LRN.
- Log each step in `PROGRESS.md`.
- Before saving, score the artifact against `rubrics/<artifact>.md`.

## Your toolkit
- `commands/` — one per step, workflow, subprocess, process and the act. Start with `operate-run-act` or the unit you're on.
- `workflows/` — run specs with checkpoints; stop at every checkpoint.
- `skills/` — how-to packages for each technique; load the ones a command names.
- `agents/` — reviewers by lens, plus researcher, synthesiser, challenger and decision-brief writer.
- `TOOLS.md` and `GUARDRAILS.md` — what you may use and must never do.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

## Scale: Solo / small
I play all the roles. Keep every output short (one page or one screen), merge steps where it makes sense, and skip formal sign-offs — but keep the decision record and the learning log.
Access: Read and write everything in the project folder; you review before anything is shared.

files.title: Accessibility reviewer
files.body:
---
name: accessibility-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Accessibility lens — Usable by people with disabilities; WCAG. Use after: 7.4.1.1 S2 Set up channels & intake; 7.4.4.1 S5 Publish, link & set a review date."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Accessibility reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at access for people with disabilities: conformance with WCAG and support for assistive technologies.

## Questions to ask
- Can people with disabilities use it?
- Did research include them?
- Which accessibility standard applies?

## Concerns to check
- Excluding users
- Legal exposure

## Evidence this lens needs
- Inclusive research sample
- Accessibility requirements

## In this act, look for
- 7.4.1.1 S2 Set up channels & intake: Intake usable with assistive technology.
- 7.4.4.1 S5 Publish, link & set a review date: Article readable with a screen reader.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

You are the AI / ML reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the use of AI and machine learning: whether a model is fit for purpose, how it's evaluated, and how bias, drift and human oversight are handled.

## Questions to ask
- Is AI actually needed here?
- How will we evaluate model quality?
- What happens when it's wrong?
- Where is human oversight?

## Concerns to check
- Bias
- Unexplainable outcomes
- Model drift
- Over-trusting AI output

## Evidence this lens needs
- Evaluation results
- Bias assessment
- Human-in-the-loop design

## In this act, look for
- 7.1.1.1 S2 Choose SLIs per journey: Accuracy is an SLI too — the parser is a model that can drift.
- 7.3.2.1 S2 Analyse candidate causes: Model behaviour on out-of-distribution inputs.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Business / Strategy reviewer
files.body:
---
name: business-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Business / Strategy lens — Strategic fit, value hypothesis, opportunity cost. Use after: 7.1.4.1 S4 Apply the policy: freeze feature releases; 7.1.4.2 S5 Send the signal pack to EVOLVE; 7.2.2.1 S3 Sev-1 or Sev-2?; 7.2.2.2 S4 Post the status page & customer notice."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Business / Strategy reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the work through the organisation's strategy: does this move a goal that matters, is it worth more than the alternatives we're giving up, and does it fit how the business creates value?

## Questions to ask
- Which strategic goal or OKR does this move?
- What's the value hypothesis — and how will we know?
- What are we not doing if we do this (opportunity cost)?
- Why now?

## Concerns to check
- Pet projects with no strategic link
- Value claimed but never measured
- Strategy drift

## Evidence this lens needs
- Linked goals / OKRs
- Value hypothesis with a measure
- Opportunity size

## In this act, look for
- 7.1.4.1 S4 Apply the policy: freeze feature releases: Sponsor told what the freeze delays.
- 7.1.4.2 S5 Send the signal pack to EVOLVE: Outcome readings reach EVOLVE on time.
- 7.2.2.1 S3 Sev-1 or Sev-2?: Does it threaten revenue or a key customer?
- 7.2.2.2 S4 Post the status page & customer notice: Key customers called personally for Sev-1.
- 7.3.4.1 S3 Rank against features: Compared honestly with features.
- 7.5.1.1 S1 Gather volumes & drivers: Sales plan and new customers included.
- 7.5.1.1 S4 Business owner agrees?: Business owner agrees the scenarios.
- 7.5.3.1 S5 Publish the report: Is the service paying its way?

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

files.title: Challenger
files.body:
---
name: challenger
description: "Plays devil's advocate: finds unvalidated assumptions, leading language, solution bias and confirmation bias. Use at: 7.1.1.1 S4 Owners agree targets & budget policy?; 7.1.2.1 S4 Dashboard matches raw events?; 7.1.3.1 S1 Derive burn-rate thresholds; 7.1.3.1 S4 Actionable and quiet enough?…."
tools: Chat
---

You are the challenger helping a person on {{initiative}}. People make every decision; you help them see clearly.

## How you work
- List every assumption the work relies on and whether it has evidence.
- Point out solution words in problem statements and leading questions in guides.
- Ask the question the team is avoiding.
- Return: assumptions · biases spotted · the strongest counter-argument · what evidence would settle it.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

files.title: Customer / User reviewer
files.body:
---
name: customer-reviewer
description: "Reviews work through the Customer / User lens — Real users, their jobs, and what adoption requires. Use after: 7.1.1.1 S1 Map critical user journeys; 7.2.1.1 S1 Receive alert or report; 7.2.2.1 S1 Assess impact & urgency; 7.2.2.1 S5 Send the first update."
tools: read-only (the files you're given)
---

You are the Customer / User reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the work from the point of view of the people who will use it or be affected by it: their jobs, pains, contexts and what adoption would really take.

## Questions to ask
- Who exactly are the users, and in which situations?
- What job are they trying to get done?
- What do they do today instead?
- What would make them switch — or refuse?

## Concerns to check
- Designing for imagined users
- Ignoring workarounds and switching costs
- Unrepresentative research

## Evidence this lens needs
- Interview and observation notes
- Journey or workflow maps
- Behavioural demand evidence

## In this act, look for
- 7.1.1.1 S1 Map critical user journeys: Drafting an order from an email is the journey, not 'the parser'.
- 7.2.1.1 S1 Receive alert or report: A clerk's report counts as much as an alert.
- 7.2.2.1 S1 Assess impact & urgency: How many users, how badly hurt?
- 7.2.2.1 S5 Send the first update: Plain-language update with the next update time.
- 7.2.2.2 S1 Draft the update from the timeline: Impact in users' terms, not system names.
- 7.2.2.2 S3 Customers affected?: Who outside the company is affected?
- 7.2.4.1 S5 Publish & raise problem records: Customer impact stated plainly.
- 7.3.1.1 S5 Rate impact & priority: How many users and orders are hurt?
- 7.3.3.1 S3 Safe and effective?: Cost to users of the workaround stated.
- 7.4.1.1 S1 Map who asks for help & how: Where do clerks ask for help today?
- 7.4.1.1 S4 Tested end to end by real users?: Real clerks tested it end to end.
- 7.4.2.1 S4 Confirm with the requester: Requester confirms it works.
- 7.4.3.1 S2 Resolved at first contact?: Answered at first contact where possible.
- 7.4.3.1 S5 Tell the user what happens next: User told what happens next.
- 7.4.4.1 S5 Publish, link & set a review date: Findable with the words users search.
- 7.6.3.1 S5 Decide & make notifications: Affected customers told plainly.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

You are the Data reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at data: what's available, its quality and lineage, what new data is needed and how it is kept, migrated and used.

## Questions to ask
- What data exists, and is it trustworthy?
- What new data will we need?
- How will we measure outcomes?
- Who owns the data?

## Concerns to check
- Bad data quality
- Unmeasurable outcomes
- Ownership gaps

## Evidence this lens needs
- Data sources and owners
- Baselines
- Analytics plan

## In this act, look for
- 7.1.2.1 S2 Instrument the gaps: Event definitions match the SLI exactly.
- 7.2.3.1 S4 Put affected data right: Data repair checked by a second person.
- 7.3.2.1 S1 Gather evidence & reproduce: Enough samples to be representative.
- 7.3.3.1 S1 Design the workaround: Workaround cannot corrupt orders.
- 7.6.2.1 S3 Write & test rules: Rules use well-defined fields.
- 7.6.3.1 S3 Contain & preserve evidence: Which data was reachable?

files.title: Decision-brief writer
files.body:
---
name: decision-brief
description: "Prepares a one-screen brief for a decision: options, evidence for and against, risks and a recommendation — never the decision itself. Use at: 7.1.1.1 S4 Owners agree targets & budget policy?; 7.1.2.1 S4 Dashboard matches raw events?; 7.1.3.1 S4 Actionable and quiet enough?; 7.1.4.1 S3 Budget left in every SLO?…."
tools: Chat
---

You are the decision-brief writer helping a person on {{initiative}}. People make every decision; you help them see clearly.

## How you work
- Restate the decision in one line and who makes it.
- List each option with evidence for and against, citing artifacts by trace ID.
- Name the main risks of each option.
- Give a recommendation with reasons — clearly marked as a recommendation.
- Never make, imply or record the decision.

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

- Can we deliver this incrementally?
- What pipeline changes are needed?

## Concerns to check
- Big-bang delivery

## Evidence this lens needs

## In this act, look for
- 7.1.3.1 S3 Test by replay and fault injection: Alerts tested like code — replay and fault injection.
- 7.1.4.1 S2 Attribute burn to causes: Which deployments spent budget?
- 7.1.4.1 S4 Apply the policy: freeze feature releases: Release manager blocks non-exempt changes.

- 7.6.1.1 S4 Set SLA & owner, raise the fix: Hotfix through the pipeline.

---

You are the Domain / Business Process reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at the business domain itself: the processes, rules, vocabulary and invariants the software must respect.

## Questions to ask
- What are the real business processes and rules here?
- What words does the business use, and what do they mean?
- Which rules can never be broken?
- Where do processes cross teams or systems?

## Concerns to check
- Software that breaks business rules
- Misunderstood vocabulary
- Hidden process steps

## Evidence this lens needs
- Current-state process / system map
- Domain rules list
- Glossary

## In this act, look for
- 7.2.2.1 S1 Assess impact & urgency: Which business process stops — order intake, picking, shipping?
- 7.2.2.2 S5 Brief service desk, sponsor & ops manager: Ops manager told which orders and sites are affected.
- 7.2.3.1 S4 Put affected data right: Wrong orders held before picking and corrected.
- 7.3.3.1 S1 Design the workaround: Workaround fits how clerks work.
- 7.4.1.1 S1 Map who asks for help & how: Which roles at each site need help, when?
- 7.4.2.1 S3 Fulfil by the request model: New PDF layouts follow the request model.
- 7.5.1.1 S1 Gather volumes & drivers: Rollout dates by site.

## Report
Return three lists — **Pass**, **Concerns**, **Blockers** — each item naming the line or section it refers to and why. Nothing else.

You are the Engineering reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at implementability: can it be built and maintained with our technology, skills and time, at sustainable quality?

## Questions to ask
- Can we build this with what we have?
- What are the technical unknowns?
- What will it cost to maintain?
- What skills are missing?

## Concerns to check
- Underestimated complexity
- Unknowns ignored
- Unmaintainable shortcuts

## Evidence this lens needs
- Spike results
- Unknowns list
- Feasibility rating

## In this act, look for
- 7.1.2.1 S2 Instrument the gaps: Instrumentation in code, reviewed like code.
- 7.2.4.1 S2 Analyse contributing factors: How did the system allow this?
- 7.3.2.1 S2 Analyse candidate causes: Candidate causes in code, config and inputs.
- 7.3.4.1 S2 Propose & estimate the fix: Fix estimated by the team that will build it.
- 7.5.4.1 S4 Apply through change enablement: Change reviewed like code.

## Report

You are the Finance / Commercial reviewer on {{initiative}}. You review; you don't rewrite the work and you don't decide. Be brief and specific.

## The lens
Looks at money: cost, funding, pricing, unit economics and the return the initiative must justify.

## Questions to ask
- What will it cost — to build and to run?
- What is the return, and over what period?
- How is it funded, and is that within limits?
- What does a unit of value cost and earn?

## Concerns to check
- Hidden run costs
- Optimistic benefits
- Unfunded commitments

## Evidence this lens needs
- Cost range including run cost
- Opportunity size
- Business case

## In this act, look for
- 7.3.4.1 S1 Cost the problem: Cost of the problem in € per month.
- 7.5.1.1 S3 Back-test against last quarter: Back-test error reported.
- 7.5.2.1 S4 Scale, tune or raise quotas: Spend within budget.
- 7.5.3.1 S1 Collect bills & usage: Every invoice and usage line collected.
- 7.5.3.1 S3 Compute unit cost & value per order: Unit cost and value per order.
- 7.5.3.1 S4 Reconciled and within target?: Reconciled to invoices.
- 7.5.4.1 S1 Find waste: Idle, oversized or duplicated spend.
- 7.5.4.1 S3 Saving worth the risk?: Is the saving worth the risk?

- Risk register
- Decision record

- 7.1.4.2 S3 Signals that need work?: Every signal ends in a decision.
- 7.2.4.1 S3 Agree owned actions: Every action owned and dated.
- 7.6.4.1 S2 Owners recertify: Owners recertify, not the security team.

---
description: "Workflow — Set SLOs & the Budget Policy"
argument-hint: <initiative> [extra context]
---

Follow AGENTS.md. Log what you do in PROGRESS.md and register new IDs in TRACE.md.
Load these skills if you can: site-reliability-engineering, golden-signals, red-method, burn-rate-calculation, service-level-management, error-budget.
Run it as specified in `workflows/operate-7-1-1-1-set-slos.md`, stopping at every checkpoint.
Context from me: $ARGUMENTS

I'm the product owner on {{initiative}}. I'm working on workflow 7.1.1.1: Set SLOs & the Budget Policy.
Goal: Turn the journeys users depend on into SLIs, set targets from real baselines and agree what happens when the budget runs out.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- Release record
- Post-deployment verification
- SLO targets
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- Service live in at least one site
- 28 days of data, or the SLO marked provisional

## What to do
Work through these steps in order. Show me the output of each step and wait for my OK before the next.
- S1. Map critical user journeys (Product owner) → Critical user journey list  [if: Journey not worth an SLO → monitor only]
- S2. Choose SLIs per journey (SRE lead) → SLI specification
- S3. Set targets from baselines (SRE lead) → SLO specification draft
- S4. ◆ DECISION — Owners agree targets & budget policy? (Service owner)  [if: Target disputed → re-derive from baseline; Owners deadlocked → sponsor]
- S5. Publish SLOs & policy (SRE lead) → Error-budget policy
At each ◆ decision, prepare the options and a recommendation — I decide.
Cases to handle: No baseline yet; Vendor-bounded journey.

## Apply
- Multi-window burn-rate alerting — Alerts on how fast an error budget is being spent, using a long window for significance and a short window to reset quickly, at several burn rates.

- Site Reliability Engineering (alerting on SLOs) — Google's discipline of running services with software-engineering methods: reliability is defined by SLOs, the gap to 100% is an error budget to spend on change, and toil is engineered away.
    How: Define SLIs from what users experience → Set SLOs below 100% and agree an error-budget policy → Alert on budget burn, not on causes → Respond to incidents with clear command and blameless postmortems → Cap toil and plan capacity ahead of demand

- Reliability / Resilience: Fast burn pages, slow burn tickets.

Goal: Turn SLO data into a release decision: spend the budget on change, or stop and fix reliability.

## What to do

## Apply
- Site Reliability Engineering (error budget policy) — Google's discipline of running services with software-engineering methods: reliability is defined by SLOs, the gap to 100% is an error budget to spend on change, and toil is engineered away.
- ISO/IEC 20000-1 (service reporting) — ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 Information technology — Service management — Part 1: Service management system requirements.
- Error budget — The amount of unreliability an SLO allows (1 − target) over its window, spent deliberately on change and protected by a policy agreed in advance.

- Signals are not defects — A metric below target is a product signal, not a bug: the capability works and the outcome hasn't arrived yet.
- Decide explicitly — Every gate ends in a named decision with an owner and a rationale — never by default.
- Trend analysis — Looking at incidents, contacts and metrics over time to find patterns before they become outages.
- Burn-rate calculation — How fast an error budget is being spent relative to spending it exactly over the window.

Run this process end to end with me, one subprocess at a time, in this order:
- 7.1.1 Define SLIs & SLOs — gate: SLO Agreement
    produces: Critical user journey list, SLO specification, Error-budget policy
- 7.1.2 Instrument & Build Dashboards — gate: Telemetry Verified
    produces: Telemetry catalogue, Service dashboard, Updated runbook
- 7.1.3 Alert on SLO Burn — gate: Alert Review

    produces: Error-budget report, Release freeze notice, Operations signal digest, Operations review minutes, Operations signal pack

After each subprocess, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate subprocess prompts if we need more depth.

## Apply
- Site Reliability Engineering — Google's discipline of running services with software-engineering methods: reliability is defined by SLOs, the gap to 100% is an error budget to spend on change, and toil is engineered away.
- ISO/IEC 20000-1 (service level management) — ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 Information technology — Service management — Part 1: Service management system requirements.
- ISO/IEC 25010 (reliability) — ISO/IEC 25010:2023 Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product quality model.
- Error budget — The amount of unreliability an SLO allows (1 − target) over its window, spent deliberately on change and protected by a policy agreed in advance.
- Multi-window burn-rate alerting — Alerts on how fast an error budget is being spent, using a long window for significance and a short window to reset quickly, at several burn rates.
- Golden signals — The four signals to watch for any user-facing system: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
- Service level management — Agreeing measurable service levels with the people who rely on a service, monitoring them and reporting honestly.
- On-call rotation — A schedule that shares responsibility for responding to pages, with escalation and limits that keep people rested.
- Measure what users feel — SLIs measure the user's experience — orders drafted, lines right — not server internals.
- Alert on symptoms, not causes — Page on user-visible symptoms (budget burn), and leave causes to dashboards and diagnosis.

- Reliability / Resilience (required)
- Operations (required)
- Concern: Measuring the wrong thing
- Concern: Alert fatigue
- Concern: Shipping into an unreliable service

- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- Alerting live
- On-call rota staffed

## What to do
Work through these steps in order. Show me the output of each step and wait for my OK before the next.
- S1. Receive alert or report (On-call engineer) → Alert
- S2. Check impact & known errors (On-call engineer) → Known-error record  [if: Known error → log with its workaround, skip diagnosis]
- S3. ◆ DECISION — Real user impact? (On-call engineer)  [if: Unclear → gather more signals; Noise → close, flag the alert for tuning]
- S4. Declare & log the incident (On-call engineer) → Incident record
- S5. Open the channel & page help (On-call engineer) → Incident timeline  [if: No answer in 5 min → secondary & SRE lead]
At each ◆ decision, prepare the options and a recommendation — I decide.
Cases to handle: Clerk reports before any alert; Several alerts from one cause.
If it fails: Log retrospectively from the timeline; Merge into the first incident.

## Apply
- Alert on symptoms, not causes — Page on user-visible symptoms (budget burn), and leave causes to dashboards and diagnosis.
- Paging tool — Routes alerts to the on-call person and escalates if unanswered.
- Known-error database — A searchable store of known errors — problems with a documented cause or symptom and a tested workaround — kept until the fix is verified.
- Change correlation — Lining up when a problem started against recent deployments, flag changes, config and vendor events.
- Service desk tool — Records contacts, requests, incidents and problems, with queues and SLAs.
- Declare early — When in doubt, declare an incident — downgrading is cheap, a late declaration is expensive.
- Incident triage — Quickly deciding what a signal is — incident, request, defect, feedback or noise — and how urgent.
- ITIL 4 (incident management) — AXELOS's framework for IT service management.
- ISO/IEC 20000-1 (incident management) — ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 Information technology — Service management — Part 1: Service management system requirements.
- Incident channel — A dedicated chat channel or bridge per incident, with the timeline kept in it.
- On-call rotation — A schedule that shares responsibility for responding to pages, with escalation and limits that keep people rested.

## Keep in mind
- Customer / User: A clerk's report counts as much as an alert.
- Support / Service Mgmt: Is there a known error with a workaround?
- Operations: When in doubt, declare.
- Operations: One owner, logged in the service desk tool.

argument-hint: <initiative> [extra context]

Context from me: $ARGUMENTS

I'm the operations lead on {{initiative}}. I'm working on workflow 7.2.3.1: Restore the Service.
Goal: Find the likely cause from telemetry and recent changes, apply the safest reversible mitigation, prove recovery on the SLIs and put affected data right.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- Incident record
- Runbook
- Deployment record
- Known-error record
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- Commander named
- Dashboard and runbook to hand

## What to do
Work through these steps in order. Show me the output of each step and wait for my OK before the next.
- S1. Form hypotheses from telemetry & changes (Operations lead) → Incident timeline
- S2. Apply the safest mitigation (On-call engineer) → Mitigation log  [if: Data repair, or no recovery in 30 min → service owner]
- S3. ◆ DECISION — SLIs recovered? (Incident commander)  [if: No recovery → next hypothesis; Cannot restore safely → controlled shutdown with comms]
- S4. Put affected data right (Ops manager) → Incident record
- S5. Resolve & request the hotfix (Incident commander) → Hotfix request
At each ◆ decision, prepare the options and a recommendation — I decide.
Cases to handle: Rollback impossible; Data already wrong.
If it fails: Reverse the last action from the mitigation log; Hold resolution until SLIs are back for 30 minutes.

## Apply
- Change correlation — Lining up when a problem started against recent deployments, flag changes, config and vendor events.
- Kepner-Tregoe problem analysis — A structured way to find a cause by comparing where the problem IS with where it COULD BE but IS NOT.
- Log store — Central, searchable store of logs with retention rules.
- Feature-flag kill switch — A runtime flag that turns a feature or path off — fully or for one segment — without a deployment.
- Graceful degradation — Designing a service to keep doing its core job, with less, when part of it fails or is overloaded.
- Circuit Breaker — Stops calling a failing dependency for a while so failures don't cascade, then tries again carefully.
- Feature-flag service — Manages runtime flags and their targeting, with an audit log.
- Restore first, diagnose later — In an incident, stop the user harm by the safest means first; the root cause can wait for the postmortem.
- Site Reliability Engineering (emergency response) — Google's discipline of running services with software-engineering methods: reliability is defined by SLOs, the gap to 100% is an error budget to spend on change, and toil is engineered away.
- ITIL 4 (incident management) — AXELOS's framework for IT service management.
- Change enablement — Getting changes into production safely and quickly by matching the scrutiny to the risk: standard changes pre-approved, normal changes assessed, emergency changes expedited.
- Incident channel — A dedicated chat channel or bridge per incident, with the timeline kept in it.
- ISO/IEC 20000-1 (incident management) — ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 Information technology — Service management — Part 1: Service management system requirements.

## Keep in mind
- DevOps / Delivery: What changed recently — deploys, flags, config?
- Vendor / Third Party: Is a vendor dependency degraded?
- DevOps / Delivery: Reversible first: flag off, roll back.
- Operations: Every action timestamped.
- Reliability / Resilience: Recovered on the SLIs, not on a hunch.
- Domain / Business Process: Wrong orders held before picking and corrected.
- Data: Data repair checked by a second person.
- Operations: Hotfix still passes the pipeline essentials.

## Rules
- Rework: No recovery → next hypothesis

## If it goes off the happy path
- Recovered → put data right and resolve
- Not recovered → next hypothesis
- Data repair → service owner
- Cannot restore → controlled shutdown

## Output

## What to do
Work through these steps in order. Show me the output of each step and wait for my OK before the next.
- S1. Reconstruct the timeline (Incident commander) → Incident timeline  [if: Sev-3/4 → short review in the record]
- S2. Analyse contributing factors (Responders) → Postmortem draft
- S3. Agree owned actions (Incident commander) → Postmortem action list  [if: Actions unfunded → service owner]
- S4. ◆ DECISION — Blameless, evidenced, actions owned? (Service owner)  [if: Blame or gaps → rewrite]
- S5. Publish & raise problem records (Incident commander) → Problem record
At each ◆ decision, prepare the options and a recommendation — I decide.
Cases to handle: Vendor-caused incident; Security incident.
If it fails: Rewrite around decisions in context and the system that allowed them; Service owner assigns owners at the review.

## Apply
- Timeline reconstruction — Rebuilding what happened, minute by minute, from logs, alerts, chat and records.
- Document repository — A versioned store for briefs, logs and supporting documents.
- Fault tree analysis — Works down from an undesired event through AND / OR gates to the combinations of causes that produce it.
- Five Whys — Ask 'why?' about five times to move from a symptom to its root cause.
- Fishbone diagram — Groups possible causes of a problem into categories along a 'fish skeleton' to find root causes.
- Causes over symptoms — Keep digging until the cause is found; complaints are symptoms.
- Retrospective — A structured, blameless look back at a piece of work to decide what to keep, stop and change — held for every outcome, including kills.
- Backlog tool — Holds the portfolio, product and iteration backlogs as linked items so every story traces up to its initiative.
- Blame the system, not the person — People act reasonably with what they know; failures come from systems that allow mistakes.
- Blameless Postmortems — A written review of an incident that explains how the system allowed it to happen, assumes people acted reasonably with what they knew, and produces owned actions.
- Site Reliability Engineering (postmortem culture) — Google's discipline of running services with software-engineering methods: reliability is defined by SLOs, the gap to 100% is an error budget to spend on change, and toil is engineered away.
- Known-error database — A searchable store of known errors — problems with a documented cause or symptom and a tested workaround — kept until the fix is verified.
- ISO/IEC 20000-1 (incident management) — ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 Information technology — Service management — Part 1: Service management system requirements.

## Keep in mind
- Operations: Timeline from logs, alerts and chat.
- Engineering: How did the system allow this?
- Security: Any security dimension?
- Reliability / Resilience: Why was detection slow?
- Governance / Risk: Every action owned and dated.
- Operations: Blameless language — decisions in context.
- Customer / User: Customer impact stated plainly.

## Rules
- Rework: Blame or gaps → rewrite the analysis

## If it goes off the happy path
- Accepted → publish and raise problems
- Blame or gaps → rewrite
- Unfunded actions → service owner
- Minor → short review

## Output
- Postmortem — a document with these sections:
    - Summary: Two or three sentences a busy reader understands.
    - Impact: Users, orders, money, SLOs.
    - Timeline: From the incident timeline.
    - Contributing factors: How the system allowed it — no names as causes.
    - What went well: Keep doing.
    - Actions: Each owned and dated.
- Postmortem action list — a table with columns: Action | Postmortem | Action | Owner | Due | Backlog link | Status

- Causes over symptoms — Keep digging until the cause is found; complaints are symptoms.
- Fault tree analysis — Works down from an undesired event through AND / OR gates to the combinations of causes that produce it.

I'm the operations lead, Communications lead on {{initiative}}. I'm working on process 7.2: Incident Management.

## What to do
Run this process end to end with me, one subprocess at a time, in this order:
- 7.2.1 Detect & Log — gate: Incident Declared
    produces: Incident record
- 7.2.2 Classify & Command — gate: Command Established
    produces: Incident command roster, Incident status update, Incident record, Customer notice
- 7.2.3 Mitigate & Restore — gate: Service Restored
    produces: Incident timeline, Resolved incident record, Hotfix request
- 7.2.4 Run the Blameless Postmortem — gate: Postmortem Accepted
    produces: Postmortem, Postmortem action list, Problem record
- In parallel: Communication runs alongside diagnosis and mitigation
- In parallel: Customer-impact clean-up ∥ diagnosis
After each subprocess, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate subprocess prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the Service Restored review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- ITIL 4 (incident management) — AXELOS's framework for IT service management.
- Incident Command System — A role-based way of running an emergency: one commander, named functional leads and a common language, adapted from emergency services to IT incidents.
- Site Reliability Engineering (emergency response) — Google's discipline of running services with software-engineering methods: reliability is defined by SLOs, the gap to 100% is an error budget to spend on change, and toil is engineered away.
- ISO/IEC 20000-1 (incident management) — ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 Information technology — Service management — Part 1: Service management system requirements.
- Severity matrix — A table that sets incident severity from business impact and says what each severity triggers.
- Feature-flag kill switch — A runtime flag that turns a feature or path off — fully or for one segment — without a deployment.
- Status page — A single place where users and stakeholders see current service status and incident updates.
- Blameless Postmortems — A written review of an incident that explains how the system allowed it to happen, assumes people acted reasonably with what they knew, and produces owned actions.
- On-call rotation — A schedule that shares responsibility for responding to pages, with escalation and limits that keep people rested.
- Restore first, diagnose later — In an incident, stop the user harm by the safest means first; the root cause can wait for the postmortem.

## Keep in mind
- Operations (required)
- Reliability / Resilience (required)
- Support / Service Mgmt (required)
- Concern: Slow detection
- Concern: Making it worse
- Concern: Customers learning before stakeholders
- Constraint: Update cadence
- Constraint: Reversible actions first

- One commander at a time
- Reversible mitigations first
- No names as causes
- Update cadence by severity
- Postmortem within 5 working days for Sev-1/2

- Evidence is weak or work fails a check → Lasting fix needed → hotfix request to BUILD
- A different valid path appears → Known error → restore with the workaround
- It goes beyond my authority → Sev-1, or no recovery in 30 minutes → service owner and executive on-call
- It should stop → Cannot restore safely → controlled shutdown with communications — recorded in the learning log

- [ ] Service restored and confirmed on the SLIs
- [ ] Affected data put right

- 7.3.1 Identify & Log Problems — gate: Problem Logged
    produces: Problem record, Incident trend report
- 7.3.2 Investigate Root Cause — gate: Root Cause Confirmed
    produces: Problem investigation, Problem record
- 7.3.3 Record Known Errors & Workarounds — gate: Known Error Published
    produces: Known-error record, Knowledge-base article, Support briefing
- 7.3.4 Rank & Resolve in the Backlog — gate: Problem Closed
    produces: Product backlog entry, Hotfix request, Fix verification

- In parallel: Reactive and proactive identification run together
After each subprocess, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate subprocess prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the Problem Review review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- ITIL 4 (problem management) — AXELOS's framework for IT service management.
- ISO/IEC 20000-1 (problem management) — ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 Information technology — Service management — Part 1: Service management system requirements.
- Known-error database — A searchable store of known errors — problems with a documented cause or symptom and a tested workaround — kept until the fix is verified.
- Multi-level backlog — Keeps work in linked backlogs at different sizes and horizons — initiatives, epics and features, stories — each owned and refined at its own cadence, so strategy traces down to the sprint and evidence traces back up.
- Operations review — A regular meeting that looks at the whole service at once — SLOs, incidents, problems, support, capacity, cost, security — and ends each item in a decision.
- Backlog refinement — A regular session where the product owner, trio and delivery team split, clarify and estimate upcoming items so they become ready.
- Causes over symptoms — Keep digging until the cause is found; complaints are symptoms.
- One backlog, one order — Problem fixes, features and improvements compete in the same ordered product backlog.
- Kepner-Tregoe problem analysis — A structured way to find a cause by comparing where the problem IS with where it COULD BE but IS NOT.
- Fault tree analysis — Works down from an undesired event through AND / OR gates to the combinations of causes that produce it.

- Operations (required)

- Product (required)
- Support / Service Mgmt (required)

- Concern: Fixes always losing to features

- Every known error links to its problem
- Problems reviewed monthly at the operations review
- Accepted problems reviewed quarterly

Run this process end to end with me, one subprocess at a time, in this order:
- 7.4.1 Run the Path to Help — gate: Path to Help Live
    produces: Path-to-help map, Support model, Service catalogue
- 7.4.2 Fulfil Service Requests — gate: Request Fulfilled
    produces: Service request, Change request

## Apply
- ITIL 4 (service desk) — AXELOS's framework for IT service management.
- Knowledge-Centred Service — The Consortium for Service Innovation's method (KCS v6) for creating and improving knowledge as a by-product of solving issues.

- Tiered support — Support organised in tiers of increasing specialism, with clear hand-offs and the aim of solving as early as possible.

- Shift-left — Moving resolution to the earliest point — self-service, then tier 1 — by giving users and agents the knowledge and tools to solve issues themselves.
- Signals are not defects — A metric below target is a product signal, not a bug: the capability works and the outcome hasn't arrived yet.
- Measure what users feel — SLIs measure the user's experience — orders drafted, lines right — not server internals.
- Incident triage — Quickly deciding what a signal is — incident, request, defect, feedback or noise — and how urgent.

- Concern: Feedback that vanishes
- Constraint: Support staffing

- A metric below target is a signal, not a defect
- Every contact gets a reply saying what happens next
- First-contact resolution tracked
- SLAs reviewed quarterly

- A different valid path appears → Known error → workaround at first contact
- It goes beyond my authority → Unhappy user or non-standard request → support lead or approver

---

argument-hint: <initiative> [extra context]
---

Run it as specified in `workflows/operate-7-5-capacity-and-cost.md`, stopping at every checkpoint.
Context from me: $ARGUMENTS

I'm the capacity planner, FinOps analyst on {{initiative}}. I'm working on process 7.5: Capacity & Cost.
Goal: Keep the service able to carry the demand that is coming, at a cost that is known, justified and no higher than it needs to be.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- Sales & volume plan
- Cloud & vendor bills
- Cost estimate
- Error-budget report
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- Service live with at least a month of volumes and bills

## What to do
Run this process end to end with me, one subprocess at a time, in this order:
- 7.5.1 Forecast Demand — gate: Forecast Agreed
    produces: Demand forecast
- 7.5.2 Plan & Test Capacity — gate: Headroom Confirmed
    produces: Capacity plan, Load-test results, Change request
- 7.5.3 Measure Cost to Serve — gate: Cost Report Accepted
    produces: Cost-to-serve report
- 7.5.4 Right-size & Optimise — gate: Saving Verified
    produces: Optimisation log, Change request
- In parallel: Cost measurement runs monthly alongside quarterly capacity planning
After each subprocess, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate subprocess prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the Capacity & Cost Review review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- ITIL 4 (capacity and performance management) — AXELOS's framework for IT service management.
- FinOps Framework — The FinOps Foundation's framework for managing the cost of cloud and technology services as a shared responsibility between engineering, finance and the business.
- ISO/IEC 20000-1 (capacity management) — ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 Information technology — Service management — Part 1: Service management system requirements.
- ISO/IEC 25010 (performance efficiency) — ISO/IEC 25010:2023 Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation (SQuaRE) — Product quality model.
- Headroom policy — A rule for how much spare capacity every resource must have at forecast peak.
- Graceful degradation — Designing a service to keep doing its core job, with less, when part of it fails or is overloaded.
- Showback — Showing each service or team the costs it incurs, without charging them, so cost becomes visible and owned.
- Capacity planning — Planning resources so forecast demand is met with headroom, before it arrives.
- Load testing — Applying realistic load to a production-like environment to prove it handles the expected peak and to find what fails first.
- Cost allocation tagging — Tagging every resource with service, environment and owner so costs can be allocated automatically.

## Keep in mind
- Infrastructure / Platform (required)
- Performance (required)
- Finance / Commercial (required)
- Concern: Saturation at peak
- Concern: Run cost drifting above value
- Constraint: Budget
- Constraint: Vendor quotas

## Rules
- Changes go through change enablement
- No optimisation while the error budget is spent
- Capacity reviewed before each peak and site rollout
- Cost reviewed monthly with finance

## If it goes off the happy path
- Evidence is weak or work fails a check → Load test fails or saving hurts an SLO → change again or roll back
- A different valid path appears → Peak cannot be met → agreed degradation plan
- It goes beyond my authority → Spend over budget or a hard vendor limit → service owner and finance
- It should stop → Not worth the risk → optimisation dropped — recorded in the learning log

## Output
- Demand forecast — a table with columns: Scenario | Orders / day (low) | Likely | High | Peak hour (likely) | Basis
    (example row: Normal (2 sites) | 950 | 1,100 | 1,250 | 210 | Sep–Oct actuals)
- Capacity plan — a table with columns: Person / role | Allocation | Leave & holidays (days, horizon) | BAU / support load | Available (focus factor 0.7) | Skills | Confirmed by | Confirmed on
    (example row: Engineer 1 | 100% | 8 | 10% | 63% | Integration, ERP API | Engineering lead | 2025-04-30)
- Load-test results — a table with columns: Scenario | Load | SLO-02 drafted < 5 min | Errors | Saturated first | Pass
    (example row: December peak hour | 340 orders/h, real anonymised PDFs | 97.5% | 0.1% | OCR API rate limit | ☑)
- Cost-to-serve report — a table with columns: Cost line | € / month | Allocation | Per order (€)
    (example row: OCR API | €1,300 | Tagged | €0.055)
- Optimisation log — a table with columns: Optimisation | Est. saving / month | SLO risk | Decision | Change | Verified saving
    (example row: Skip OCR for PDFs with a text layer (≈ 40%) | €520 | Low | Do | CHG-049 | €505)

## Before you finish, check
- [ ] Headroom ≥ 30% at forecast peak hour
- [ ] ≥ 95% of spend allocated
- [ ] Unit cost and value per order stated
- [ ] Peak proven with headroom
- [ ] Cost-to-serve report accepted by finance
- [ ] Savings verified

files.body:
---
description: "Workflow — Triage & Fix a Vulnerability"
argument-hint: <initiative> [extra context]
---

Follow AGENTS.md. Log what you do in PROGRESS.md and register new IDs in TRACE.md.
Load these skills if you can: nist-cybersecurity-framework, epss, risk-based-vulnerability-prioritisation, patch-management, feature-flag-kill-switch.
Run it as specified in `workflows/operate-7-6-1-1-vulnerability.md`, stopping at every checkpoint.
Context from me: $ARGUMENTS

I'm the security analyst on {{initiative}}. I'm working on workflow 7.6.1.1: Triage & Fix a Vulnerability.
Goal: Match each finding to what actually runs, judge exploitability and exposure, set an SLA and owner, and verify the fix by rescanning.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- SBOM
- Security advisory
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- SBOM current for the running release

## What to do
Work through these steps in order. Show me the output of each step and wait for my OK before the next.
- S1. Match findings to the SBOM (Security analyst) → Scanner findings
- S2. Assess exploitability & exposure (Security analyst) → Vulnerability record
- S3. ◆ DECISION — Affects us above threshold? (Security analyst)  [if: Not affected → VEX statement & close]
- S4. Set SLA & owner, raise the fix (Security lead) → Hotfix request  [if: SLA can't be met → exception by service owner & security lead]
- S5. Verify by rescan & close (Security analyst) → Vulnerability register  [if: Rescan still finds it → redo]
At each ◆ decision, prepare the options and a recommendation — I decide.
Cases to handle: Code path unused; No fix available.
If it fails: Daily review of SLA breaches by the security lead; Reopen and rescan.

## Apply
- Vulnerability scanner — Scans images, dependencies and hosts for known vulnerabilities against the SBOM.
- NIST Cybersecurity Framework (identify and protect) — NIST's framework (CSF 2.0) organising cybersecurity outcomes into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
- CVSS — The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (FIRST, v4.0): a 0–10 score of a vulnerability's technical severity from its base, threat and environmental metrics.
- EPSS — The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (FIRST): the probability a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days.
- Risk-based vulnerability prioritisation — Ordering vulnerability fixes by real risk — exploitability, exposure and impact — not by CVSS score alone.
- Defence in depth — Layer independent controls so one failure does not expose the service.
- Patch management — Applying security and stability patches on a schedule set by risk, verified and recorded.
- Feature-flag kill switch — A runtime flag that turns a feature or path off — fully or for one segment — without a deployment.
- ISO/IEC 27001 (technical vulnerability management) — ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Information security management systems — Requirements.

## Keep in mind
- Security: Findings matched to what actually runs (SBOM).
- Security: Exploitability and exposure, not CVSS alone.
- Vendor / Third Party: Vendor-hosted components included.
- Security: Above threshold → SLA by risk.
- DevOps / Delivery: Hotfix through the pipeline.
- Operations: Redeploy within the error budget where possible.
- Compliance / Regulatory: Evidence kept for audit.

## Rules
- Rework: Rescan still finds it → redo the fix

## If it goes off the happy path
- Affected → SLA, owner, hotfix
- Not affected → VEX and close
- SLA impossible → exception
- Rescan fails → redo

## Output
- Vulnerability register — a table with columns: ID | CVE / finding | Component | CVSS | Known exploited | Exposure | SLA | Owner | Status
    (example row: VUL-021 | CVE-2025-XXXX heap overflow | pdf-render-lib 4.2.1 | 9.8 | ☑ | Internet (email attachments) | 72 h | Dev lead | Verified (DEP-036, 30 h))
- Hotfix request — fill these fields: Raised from; Problem to fix; Proposed fix; Why it can't wait; Acceptance; Becomes; Approved by
- Security exception — fill these fields: Vulnerability; Why the SLA can't be met; Mitigating controls; Residual risk (High / Medium / Low); Expires; Approved by

## Before you finish, check
- [ ] SLA set by risk
- [ ] Exposure assessed
- [ ] Fixed and verified, or excepted

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

## What to do
1. Assess exploitability & exposure.
2. Use CVSS and EPSS and Risk-based vulnerability prioritisation (see "Apply" below).
3. Write the result as the Vulnerability record, in the output format below.

## Apply
- CVSS — The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (FIRST, v4.0): a 0–10 score of a vulnerability's technical severity from its base, threat and environmental metrics.
    How: Read the base score from the advisory → Adjust for threat (is it exploited?) → Adjust for your environment (exposure, mitigations) → Combine with EPSS and known-exploited lists to prioritise
- EPSS — The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (FIRST): the probability a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days.
    How: Look up the EPSS score → Combine with CVSS, exposure and known-exploited status
- Risk-based vulnerability prioritisation — Ordering vulnerability fixes by real risk — exploitability, exposure and impact — not by CVSS score alone.
    How: Is the component actually used? → Is it exposed? → Is it exploited in the wild (KEV) or likely to be (EPSS)? → What would an attacker gain? → Set SLA by the result

## Keep in mind
- Security: Exploitability and exposure, not CVSS alone.
- Vendor / Third Party: Vendor-hosted components included.

I'm the security analyst on {{initiative}}. I'm working on subprocess 7.6.1: Manage Vulnerabilities.
Goal: Find the vulnerabilities that matter in what we run, and fix them within a time set by risk.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching
- SBOM
- Security advisory
- {{anything else relevant}}

## Before we start
Check these are true, or tell me what's missing:
- SBOM for the running release
- Scanner and advisory feeds into the register

## What to do
Run this subprocess end to end with me, one workflow at a time, in this order:
- 7.6.1.1 Triage & Fix a Vulnerability — gate: Remediation Within SLA
    produces: Vulnerability register, Hotfix request, Security exception
- In parallel: Many findings triaged in parallel
After each workflow, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate workflow prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the Remediation Within SLA review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- NIST Cybersecurity Framework (identify and protect) — NIST's framework (CSF 2.0) organising cybersecurity outcomes into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
- CVSS — The Common Vulnerability Scoring System (FIRST, v4.0): a 0–10 score of a vulnerability's technical severity from its base, threat and environmental metrics.
- ISO/IEC 27001 (technical vulnerability management) — ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Information security management systems — Requirements.
- Feature-flag kill switch — A runtime flag that turns a feature or path off — fully or for one segment — without a deployment.
- Patch management — Applying security and stability patches on a schedule set by risk, verified and recorded.
- Defence in depth — Layer independent controls so one failure does not expose the service.
- Risk-based vulnerability prioritisation — Ordering vulnerability fixes by real risk — exploitability, exposure and impact — not by CVSS score alone.
- EPSS — The Exploit Prediction Scoring System (FIRST): the probability a vulnerability will be exploited in the next 30 days.
- Vulnerability scanner — Scans images, dependencies and hosts for known vulnerabilities against the SBOM.

## Keep in mind
- Security (required)
- Operations (required)
- Concern: Known-exploited flaws left open
- Constraint: Patch windows
- Constraint: Error budget for redeploys

## Rules
- Every exception time-limited and owned
- Base images rebuilt weekly
- SBOM kept current per release

## If it goes off the happy path
- Evidence is weak or work fails a check → Fix fails verification → redo
- A different valid path appears → Not affected → VEX statement
- It goes beyond my authority → SLA cannot be met → security exception from service owner and security lead
- It should stop → False positive → closed with the reason — recorded in the learning log

## Output
- Vulnerability register — a table with columns: ID | CVE / finding | Component | CVSS | Known exploited | Exposure | SLA | Owner | Status
    (example row: VUL-021 | CVE-2025-XXXX heap overflow | pdf-render-lib 4.2.1 | 9.8 | ☑ | Internet (email attachments) | 72 h | Dev lead | Verified (DEP-036, 30 h))

- S2. Onboard log sources (Platform engineer) → Log-source inventory  [if: Log source missing → platform owner]
- S3. Write & test rules (Security analyst) → Detection rules
- S4. ◆ DECISION — Fires on test, quiet in normal traffic? (Security lead)  [if: Fails test or noisy → rewrite]

Cases to handle: Crafted PDF attachment; Month-end bulk imports.
If it fails: Re-test monthly with the attack simulation; Add context conditions and thresholds.

## Apply
- Threat-informed detection — Choosing what to detect from the threats the threat model rates highest and the techniques attackers use.
- Assume breach — Design operations as if an attacker is already inside: detect, limit and recover, not only prevent.
- NIST Cybersecurity Framework (detect) — NIST's framework (CSF 2.0) organising cybersecurity outcomes into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
- Log store — Central, searchable store of logs with retention rules.
- Defence in depth — Layer independent controls so one failure does not expose the service.
- Detection as code — Security detection rules written, reviewed, tested and deployed like code.
- SIEM — Security information and event management: collects security logs, runs detections and supports investigation.
- Fault injection — Deliberately introducing a fault to check that alerts, runbooks and defences respond as intended.
- Game day — A planned exercise that simulates a failure or attack in a controlled way to test people, runbooks and detections.
- ISO/IEC 27001 (logging and monitoring) — ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Information security management systems — Requirements.

## Keep in mind
- Security: Each high threat from the threat model covered.
- Privacy: No personal data in security logs beyond need.
- Infrastructure / Platform: Log sources reliable and complete.
- Data: Rules use well-defined fields.
- Security: Fires on simulation, quiet otherwise.
- Operations: Routed to someone who will act.

## Rules
- Rework: Fails test or noisy → rewrite

## If it goes off the happy path
- Pass → live
- Fail or noisy → rewrite
- Log source missing → platform owner
- Low threat → no rule

## Output
- Detection rule catalogue — a table with columns: Detection | Threat | Logic | Log sources | Last tested | Route
    (example row: ALR-11 | THR-05 | ERP import token used from an unknown IP | API gateway, identity provider | 2025-10-01 | Security triage)

- [ ] Rules live and routed

I'm the SRE lead, Support lead, Problem manager, Security lead on {{initiative}}. Help me run this act end to end.
Goal: Run the service reliably, securely and economically for its users, respond to failure, and turn operational signals into knowledge and work.
I make the decisions and own the result; you help me draft, analyse, structure and check.

## Context I'm attaching

## Before we start

- Runbooks, dashboards baseline and support handover received from RELEASE
- SLO targets from DESIGN's quality-attribute scenarios

## What to do
Run this act end to end with me, one process at a time, in this order:
- 7.1 Observability & Monitoring — gate: SLO & Error Budget
    produces: SLO specification, Error-budget policy, Service dashboard, Alert rules, On-call rota, Error-budget report, Release freeze notice, Operations signal digest, Operations signal pack
- 7.2 Incident Management — gate: Service Restored
    produces: Incident record, Incident status update, Incident timeline, Hotfix request, Postmortem, Problem record
- 7.3 Problem Management — gate: Problem Review
    produces: Problem record, Problem investigation, Known-error record, Knowledge-base article, Product backlog entry, Fix verification
- 7.4 Service Request & Support — gate: Support Service Review
    produces: Service catalogue, Support model, Service request, Feedback record, Knowledge-base article, Support report
- 7.5 Capacity & Cost — gate: Capacity & Cost Review
    produces: Demand forecast, Capacity plan, Load-test results, Cost-to-serve report, Optimisation log
- 7.6 Security Operations — gate: Security Posture Review
    produces: Vulnerability register, Detection rule catalogue, Security event record, Breach notification, Access review, Security posture report, Hotfix request
- In parallel: All six processes run continuously and concurrently while the service is live
- In parallel: Incident (7.2) and security response (7.6.3) share incident command
- In parallel: Monthly operations review joins them: SLOs, incidents, problems, support, capacity, security
After each process, summarise what we produced, list open questions and assumptions, and wait for my go-ahead. Use the separate process prompts if we need more depth.
At the end, prepare the SLO & Error Budget review: check our evidence against the criteria below and recommend forward, rework or stop. I decide.

## Apply
- Site Reliability Engineering — Google's discipline of running services with software-engineering methods: reliability is defined by SLOs, the gap to 100% is an error budget to spend on change, and toil is engineered away.
- ITIL 4 — AXELOS's framework for IT service management.
- NIST Cybersecurity Framework — NIST's framework (CSF 2.0) organising cybersecurity outcomes into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
- FinOps Framework — The FinOps Foundation's framework for managing the cost of cloud and technology services as a shared responsibility between engineering, finance and the business.
- ISO/IEC 20000-1 — ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 Information technology — Service management — Part 1: Service management system requirements.
- ISO/IEC 27001 — ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Information security management systems — Requirements.
- NIST SP 800-61 — NIST Special Publication 800-61 — Computer Security Incident Handling Guide (Rev.
- Error budget — The amount of unreliability an SLO allows (1 − target) over its window, spent deliberately on change and protected by a policy agreed in advance.
- Known-error database — A searchable store of known errors — problems with a documented cause or symptom and a tested workaround — kept until the fix is verified.
- Blameless Postmortems — A written review of an incident that explains how the system allowed it to happen, assumes people acted reasonably with what they knew, and produces owned actions.

## Keep in mind
- Operations (required)
- Reliability / Resilience (required)
- Support / Service Mgmt (required)
- Security (required)
- Concern: Users hurt before we notice
- Concern: The same failure recurring
- Concern: Run cost drifting above value
- Concern: Known-exploited flaws left open
- Constraint: Error budgets
- Constraint: On-call capacity
- Constraint: Vendor limits and quotas
- Constraint: Legal notification deadlines

## Rules
- Budget spent → only reliability fixes and security patches release
- No silent fixes of user-visible failures
- A metric below target is a signal, not a defect
- Whoever records readings does not judge them
- On-call is staffed, rested and paid
- Postmortems are blameless
- Production data used for analysis only anonymised

## If it goes off the happy path
- Evidence is weak or work fails a check → Fix needed now → hotfix request to BUILD
- A different valid path appears → Known error → workaround restores service while the fix waits
- It goes beyond my authority → Severity breach or SLA breach → incident command, service owner; personal-data breach → DPO
- It should stop → Budget spent → feature releases frozen; only reliability fixes and security patches ship until the SLO recovers and the service owner lifts the freeze — recorded in the learning log

## Output
- SLO specification — a table with columns: SLO | Journey | SLI: good events / valid events | Target | Window | Error budget | Owner | Source
    (example row: SLO-01 | Order becomes a draft | Emails with a PDF imported without system error / emails with a PDF | 99.5% | 28 days | 0.5% (≈ 110 orders) | SRE lead | QAS-04)
- Service dashboard — sections: SLO-01 import success, SLO-02 drafted < 5 min, SLO-03 lines right, Golden signals, Recent changes
- Alert rules — a table with columns: Alert | SLO | Condition | Severity | Route | Runbook step
    (example row: ALR-01 | SLO-01 | Burn 14.4× over 1 h and 5 min | Page | On-call primary | RB §3.1)
- Incident record — fill these fields: Incident ID; Detected by (Alert / User report / Monitoring / Other); Declared; Severity (Sev-1 / Sev-2 / Sev-3 / Sev-4); Impact; Commander; Mitigation; Restored; Data put right; Linked; Status (Open / Mitigated / Resolved / Closed)
- Postmortem — a document with these sections:
    - Summary: Two or three sentences a busy reader understands.
    - Impact: Users, orders, money, SLOs.
    - Timeline: From the incident timeline.
    - Contributing factors: How the system allowed it — no names as causes.
    - What went well: Keep doing.
    - Actions: Each owned and dated.
- Problem record — fill these fields: Problem ID; Linked incidents; Symptom; Root cause; Impact (High / Medium / Low); Proposed fix; Added to product backlog
- Known-error record — fill these fields: Known error ID; Problem; Symptom users see; Workaround; Cost of workaround; Tested by; KB article; Retire when
- Service request — fill these fields: Ticket ID; From; Type (Question / Request / Incident / Defect / Feedback); What they asked; Catalogue offering; Triage decision; Became; Opened; Closed; Requester confirmed
- Knowledge-base article — a document with these sections:
    - Issue: In the user's words.
    - Environment: Where it applies.
    - Resolution: Steps that work.
    - Cause: Why it happens.
- Capacity report — a table with columns: Resource / quota | Limit | At forecast peak | Headroom | Policy ≥ 30% | Action
    (example row: Parser workers (CPU) | Autoscale 2–12 | 7 workers | 42% | ☑ | —)
- Cost-to-serve report — a table with columns: Cost line | € / month | Allocation | Per order (€)
    (example row: OCR API | €1,300 | Tagged | €0.055)
- Vulnerability register — a table with columns: ID | CVE / finding | Component | CVSS | Known exploited | Exposure | SLA | Owner | Status
    (example row: VUL-021 | CVE-2025-XXXX heap overflow | pdf-render-lib 4.2.1 | 9.8 | ☑ | Internet (email attachments) | 72 h | Dev lead | Verified (DEP-036, 30 h))
- Security event record — fill these fields: Alert; Detected; Triage (False positive / Suspicious / Confirmed); Scope; Containment; Evidence preserved; Personal data involved (Yes / No / Unknown); Incident
- Error-budget report — a document with these sections:
    - Summary: One line per SLO: attainment and budget used.
    - Burn attribution: What spent each budget, with IDs.
    - Policy decision: Continue, slow down or freeze.
    - Exemptions: Anything excluded and why.
    - Signals for EVOLVE: Outcome readings and patterns.
    - Decision: Continue / Slow down / Freeze
- Hotfix request — fill these fields: Raised from; Problem to fix; Proposed fix; Why it can't wait; Acceptance; Becomes; Approved by
- Operations signal pack — a pack with: Error-budget report, Operations signal digest, Postmortem, Problem record, Cost-to-serve report, Security posture report
- Learning log — a table with columns: Learning ID | Date | From (unit / decision) | What happened | What we learned | Change we'll make | Type | Owner | Applied?
    (example row: LRN-007 | 2025-04-02 | DEC-012 · Discovery Decision | Go with condition on vendor connector | Vendor dependency surfaced late (1.5) — should be scanned in 1.4 | Add vendor-support check to Existing Solutions scan | Retrospective | Product manager | ☐)

## Before you finish, check
- [ ] Every critical journey has an SLO with an error-budget policy
- [ ] Every Sev-1/2 incident has a published blameless postmortem
- [ ] Every recurring cause has a problem record ranked in the product backlog
- [ ] Vulnerabilities fixed within their risk-based SLA
- [ ] The service is retired (EVOLVE decision) — OPERATE otherwise runs continuously
- [ ] Each month: error-budget report published and the policy applied
- [ ] Each cycle: signals handed to EVOLVE

## Ground rules
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.

files.title: Guardrails & hooks
files.body:
# Guardrails & hooks — Operate

People own the work, agents help do it. In every unit the person in the role briefs the agent, gives it the right context, checks what it produces, and makes every decision. The agent drafts, researches, analyses, structures and checks — it never decides, approves or signs.

## Always
- Don't invent facts, figures, quotes or sources — mark anything unverified as an assumption.
- If something you need is missing, ask me instead of guessing.
- Keep personal or confidential data out unless I've provided it for this purpose.
- Prepare decisions; don't make them — I decide.
- Never paste passwords, keys, or personal data you aren't allowed to share — anonymise first
- At enterprise scale, use only approved tools
- Check every fact, number and source the agent gives you
- Agents prepare decisions; people make them
- Save the output in the artifact template and note that an agent helped
- If the agent's output is wrong, correct the prompt or the context — then record what you learned

## Scale: Solo / small
- Read and write everything in the project folder; you review before anything is shared.
- Watch for: Skipping discovery because 'I already know'
- Watch for: Accepting agent output unreviewed because there's no one else to check it

## Hooks — automatic where your agent supports them, a checklist everywhere else
| When | Check | If it fails |
|---|---|---|
| Before saving an artifact | It follows its template · it carries its trace ID and links upstream IDs · every claim cites evidence or is marked 'Assumption:' · no personal data or secrets | Fix, or stop and tell me |
| Before a decision step | Stop. Prepare the decision brief. Wait for the named decision-maker | Never decide or approve |
| Before anything leaves the team | Messages, posts, invitations and shared documents are drafts until a person sends them | Ask for approval |
| Before using a new tool or data source | Is it allowed at this scale? Is the data allowed in this tool? | Ask first |
| After each step | Append to PROGRESS.md: date, unit, what was done, artifacts, decisions, open questions, next | Always |

## Rules and policies by unit
### OPERATE
- Budget spent → only reliability fixes and security patches release
- No silent fixes of user-visible failures
- A metric below target is a signal, not a defect
- Whoever records readings does not judge them
- On-call is staffed, rested and paid
- Postmortems are blameless
- Production data used for analysis only anonymised
- Error budgets
- On-call capacity
- Vendor limits and quotas
- Legal notification deadlines

### 7.1 Observability & Monitoring
- No SLO at 100%
- Budget spent → only reliability fixes and security patches release
- SLOs reviewed quarterly
- On-call load ≤ 2 pages per shift on average
- Telemetry cost
- No personal data in logs

### 7.1.1 Define SLIs & SLOs
- An SLO without an error-budget policy is not agreed
- Never set an SLO at 100%
- SLOs reviewed at least quarterly
- Any external SLA looser than the internal SLO
- What can be measured today

### 7.1.2 Instrument & Build Dashboards
- No personal data or order contents in logs, labels or traces
- OpenTelemetry naming conventions
- Log retention follows the data policy
- Telemetry cost
- No personal data in logs

### 7.1.3 Alert on SLO Burn
- Every page is actionable
- No alert without an owner
- On-call load: at most 2 pages per shift on average
- On-call is paid and rested per policy
- On-call capacity

### 7.1.4 Track the Error Budget
- Budget spent → only reliability fixes and security patches release
- Whoever recorded the readings does not judge them
- Freeze lifted only by the service owner
- Report monthly and at every gate decision
- Policy agreed in advance, not during the argument

### 7.2 Incident Management
- One commander at a time
- Reversible mitigations first
- No names as causes
- Update cadence by severity
- Postmortem within 5 working days for Sev-1/2
- Update cadence
- Reversible actions first

### 7.2.1 Detect & Log
- When in doubt, declare — downgrading is cheap
- No silent fixes of user-visible failures
- All incidents logged in the service desk tool
- Clerk reports count as detection signals
- Paging policy

### 7.2.2 Classify & Command
- The commander coordinates and does not debug
- Hand-overs of command are announced
- Updates every 30 min for Sev-1/2 and every 2 h for Sev-3
- Customer notices approved by the communications lead
- Update cadence

### 7.2.3 Mitigate & Restore
- Prefer reversible mitigations: flag off, roll back, fail over
- No data repair without the commander's approval
- Hotfixes still pass the pipeline and the DoD essentials
- Affected customers' data put right before close
- Reversible actions first

### 7.2.4 Run the Blameless Postmortem
- No names as causes; describe decisions in their context
- Unresolved causes become problem records
- Postmortem within 5 working days for Sev-1/2
- Actions reviewed at the operations review
- 5-day deadline

### 7.3 Problem Management
- One backlog, one order — no side queue for fixes
- Every known error links to its problem
- Problems reviewed monthly at the operations review
- Accepted problems reviewed quarterly
- Investigation timebox
- Sprint capacity

### 7.3.1 Identify & Log Problems
- One problem record per cause
- Problems reviewed monthly at the operations review
- Problem manager capacity

### 7.3.2 Investigate Root Cause
- Evidence before conclusions
- Investigation timeboxed (10 working days by default)
- Production data used only anonymised
- Investigation timebox

### 7.3.3 Record Known Errors & Workarounds
- Every known error links to its problem record
- Retired when the fix is verified
- Known errors searchable from the service desk tool
- Clerk time

### 7.3.4 Rank & Resolve in the Backlog
- One backlog, one order — no side queue for fixes
- Close only on evidence of no recurrence
- Problem items ranked with WSJF like features
- Accepted problems reviewed quarterly
- Sprint capacity

### 7.4 Service Request & Support
- A metric below target is a signal, not a defect
- Every contact gets a reply saying what happens next
- First-contact resolution tracked
- SLAs reviewed quarterly
- Support staffing
- Response SLAs

### 7.4.1 Run the Path to Help
- No help through personal inboxes
- Intake meets WCAG 2.2 AA
- SLAs reviewed quarterly against the support report
- Support staffing

### 7.4.2 Fulfil Service Requests
- Access requests follow least privilege
- Standard requests need no extra approval
- Every request logged, even if solved on the phone
- SLA

### 7.4.3 Triage Questions & Feedback
- A metric below target is a signal, not a defect
- Every contact gets a reply saying what happens next
- First-contact resolution tracked
- Feedback records reviewed weekly by the product owner
- Response SLA

### 7.4.4 Maintain the Knowledge Base
- No personal data or secrets in articles
- Articles reviewed every 6 months and when their fix ships
- Article reuse counted
- Reviewer time

### 7.5 Capacity & Cost
- Changes go through change enablement
- No optimisation while the error budget is spent
- Capacity reviewed before each peak and site rollout
- Cost reviewed monthly with finance
- Budget
- Vendor quotas

### 7.5.1 Forecast Demand
- Every assumption sourced
- Forecast refreshed quarterly and before each site rollout
- Length of data history

### 7.5.2 Plan & Test Capacity
- Changes go through change enablement
- No load testing against the production ERP
- Plan reviewed before each site rollout and each peak
- Budget
- Vendor quotas

### 7.5.3 Measure Cost to Serve
- Every resource tagged with service and environment
- Monthly report; quarterly review with finance
- Budget

### 7.5.4 Right-size & Optimise
- No optimisation while the error budget is spent
- Clerk time counts as cost
- Optimisation log reviewed monthly
- Error budget

### 7.6 Security Operations
- Least privilege
- Evidence preserved before containment changes
- Personal-data breaches assessed within 72 hours
- Exceptions time-limited and owned
- Security logs kept 12 months
- 72-hour notification clock
- Patch windows

### 7.6.1 Manage Vulnerabilities
- Every exception time-limited and owned
- Base images rebuilt weekly
- SBOM kept current per release
- Patch windows
- Error budget for redeploys

### 7.6.2 Monitor Security Events
- No credentials or personal data in rule outputs
- Detection rules version-controlled
- Security logs kept 12 months
- Log costs
- Personal data in logs

### 7.6.3 Respond to Security Incidents
- Personal-data breaches assessed for notification within 72 hours
- Chain of custody for evidence
- Security incidents run under incident command
- Restricted distribution of details
- 72-hour clock

### 7.6.4 Review Access & Posture
- Least privilege
- No shared personal accounts
- Quarterly recertification
- Evidence kept 3 years for audit
- Audit timetable
